跟着在东京工作的ヤン和朋友美咲去京都、城崎温泉：坐新干线、住旅馆、找失物、遇台风: Travel to Kyoto and Kinosaki Onsen with Yang, who works in Tokyo, and her friend Misaki: ride the shinkansen, stay at a ryokan, track down a lost item, and get caught in a typhoon. Learn Japanese for the road that is both polite and warm.
在东京站问路和换乘: Asking the way and changing trains at Tokyo Station
十一月一个星期六的早上八点，在东京工作的ヤン要和朋友美咲一起坐新干线去京都。她一: It's 8 a.m. on a Saturday in November. Yang, who works in Tokyo, is about to take the shinkansen to Kyoto with her friend Misaki. She has come ahead on her own on the Chuo Line and arrived at Tokyo Station, which is packed with people and crammed with signs. She hasn't bought her shinkansen ticket yet and can't find the transfer gate, so she heads over to a station attendant by the ticket gates.
东京站检票口旁的站员，五十岁左右，一早上已经被问了几十次路，依然很耐心: A station attendant by the ticket gates at Tokyo Station, around fifty; he has already been asked for directions dozens of times this morning but is still very patient
在东京IT公司工作第三年的中国人，二十八岁，日语日常够用，第一次去京都旅行: A 28-year-old from China in her third year at an IT company in Tokyo; her Japanese is good enough for everyday life, and this is her first trip to Kyoto
站员和乘客是陌生人之间的服务关系。站员用简洁的丁宁语，偶尔带一点尊敬语；ヤン只要: The station attendant and the passenger are strangers in a service relationship. The attendant uses concise polite (です/ます) speech, with a touch of honorific language (sonkeigo) now and then. Yang only needs to ask politely in the 「です・ます」 style; there's no need for complicated keigo. What matters is to greet him first, say clearly where you want to go, and thank him properly at the end.
不好意思，可以打扰一下吗？: Excuse me, do you have a moment?
问路前先用「すみません」叫住对方，再加一句「ちょっといいですか」，等于给对方一秒: Before asking for directions, first use 「すみません」 to get the person's attention, then add 「ちょっといいですか」; this gives them a second to get ready. Station attendants are often dealing with something else at the same time, and rushing up out of nowhere to ask 「新幹線は？」 comes across as impatient.
您好，怎么了？: Yes, how can I help you?
我想坐新干线，可是还没买票。: I'd like to take the shinkansen, but I haven't bought a ticket yet.
「〜たいんですが」是把自己的情况先摆出来，后半句留给对方接。比直接说「切符はどこ: 「〜たいんですが」 lays out your situation first and leaves the rest of the sentence for the other person to pick up. Compared with asking 「切符はどこですか」 outright, it sounds more like you're asking for advice, and the other person will naturally help you work out the next step.
车票的话，可以在绿色窗口或者那边的售票机买。: If it's a ticket you need, you can buy one at the Midori no Madoguchi ticket office or at the ticket machines over there.
绿色窗口在哪里？: Where is the Midori no Madoguchi?
顺着这条通道直走，在右手边。绿色的招牌就是标志。: Go straight down this passage, and it's on the right. Look for the green sign.
直走，然后右边，对吧。: So straight ahead, and then it's on the right?
把听到的路线用短句复述一遍，句尾加「ね」确认。这样站员能马上纠正你听错的地方，也: Repeat the route you heard back in a short phrase, and add 「ね」 at the end to confirm. That way the attendant can immediately correct anything you misheard, and he'll also see that you were really listening. Stations are noisy, and repeating it back once is more useful than saying 「わかりました」 ten times.
对。买好票以后，请从前面的新干线换乘口进去。: Yes, that's right. Once you've bought your ticket, go in through the shinkansen transfer gate just past it.
明白了。去京都的车在几号站台？: I see. Which track do trains to Kyoto leave from?
根据车次不同，在十四号到十九号站台。请在里面的电子显示屏上确认一下。: It depends on the train, but it's one of Tracks 14 through 19. Please check the electronic departure board inside.
「〜によって違います」是“看情况而定”的标准说法。站员不会替你记住车次，而是告诉: 「〜によって違います」 is the standard way to say "it depends." The attendant won't keep track of your train for you; instead, he tells you where to go to check for yourself. Nearly all station information in Japan is on the display boards, so once you learn to read 「番線」 (track number), 「発車時刻」 (departure time), and 「号車」 (car number), you'll have nothing to worry about.
电子显示屏是吧。谢谢您。: The electronic board, got it. Thank you very much.
不客气。路上小心。: Not at all. Have a safe trip.
您这么忙还帮我，谢谢了。: Thank you for your help when you're so busy.
离开前再加一句「お忙しいところ」，是在说“我知道你很忙”。早上的东京站，站员几乎: Adding 「お忙しいところ」 before you leave is a way of saying "I know you're busy." At Tokyo Station in the morning, the attendants hardly have a moment to stop, and this one phrase lets them feel that their hard work has been noticed.
称呼时说「すみません」就行，不用叫「駅員さん」: To get their attention, just say 「すみません」; there's no need to call them 「駅員さん」
「切符を買う」；新干线要「乗車券」和「特急券」两种: 「切符を買う」 (to buy a ticket); for the shinkansen you need two kinds: a 「乗車券」 (basic fare ticket) and a 「特急券」 (limited express ticket)
JR绿色窗口（人工售票处）: JR's "green window" ticket office (staffed ticket counter)
复杂的票、学生优惠、改签都在这里办: This is where you handle complicated tickets, student discounts, and ticket changes
「券売機で買う」；大多有中文和英文画面: 「券売機で買う」 (to buy from a ticket machine); most have Chinese and English screens
从JR普通线换到新干线时要经过的专用检票口: The dedicated ticket gate you pass through when transferring from regular JR lines to the shinkansen
「改札を出る」= 出站，「改札の前で待ち合わせ」很常用: 「改札を出る」 = to exit the station (through the gates); 「改札の前で待ち合わせ」 (meeting in front of the ticket gates) is very common
「何番線ですか」= 在几号站台；广播里也常听到: 「何番線ですか」 = Which track is it?; you'll also hear it often in announcements
「この通路をまっすぐ」；指路时常和「突き当たり」一起出现: 「この通路をまっすぐ」 (straight down this passage); when giving directions, it often comes up together with 「突き当たり」 (the end of the passage)
「まっすぐ行く」；问路时最常听到的词之一: 「まっすぐ行く」 (to go straight); one of the words you hear most often when asking for directions
「右側にあります」；左手边是「左側」: 「右側にあります」 (it's on the right); the left side is 「左側」
「〜が目印です」= 看到……就是了；约见面时也常用: 「〜が目印です」 = look for ... and you've found it; also often used when arranging where to meet
显示车次、站台、发车时间；站员常说「掲示板で確認して」: Shows trains, tracks, and departure times; station staff often say 「掲示板で確認して」 (check the board)
比「電車」正式，站员、广播常用: More formal than 「電車」; often used by station staff and in announcements
我想……（可是不知道怎么办）: I'd like to ... (but I'm not sure what to do)
动词ます形去ます + たいんですが: Verb ます-stem + たいんですが
「んです」是在说明自己的情况，「が」把话留了一半，意思是“您能帮我一下吗”。在车: 「んです」 explains your situation, and 「が」 leaves the sentence half-finished, with the meaning "could you help me?" When asking for help at a station, in a shop, or at a counter, it's the most natural way to begin. Saying 「〜したいです」 outright sounds like announcing a wish, and the other person won't know what you want them to do.
我想去京都……: I'd like to go to Kyoto...
我想买票，可是不会用。: I'd like to buy a ticket, but I don't know how to use this.
把听到的关键词 + ですね: Key word(s) you heard + ですね
日本人说话很重视“确认”。把对方说的关键信息重复一遍再加「ね」，既是确认，也是在: Japanese speakers place a lot of weight on "confirming." Repeating the key information the other person said and adding 「ね」 both confirms it and tells them "I've understood." It's the same at a station or when answering the phone at work: every time you confirm, there's one less chance of a mistake.
第二个路口左转对吧。: Left at the second corner, is that right?
在车站、商场、街上向陌生人问路时都可以这样问：先「すみません」叫住对方，再说「〜: You can ask this way whenever you ask a stranger for directions, whether at a station, in a shopping mall, or on the street: first get their attention with 「すみません」, then explain your situation with 「〜たいんですが」, and finally repeat back what you heard to confirm and say thank you.
不要一上来就只说一个词「新幹線？」或拿着手机屏幕往对方眼前一伸。中国人习惯直接问: Don't open with just a single word like 「新幹線？」, or thrust your phone screen in front of the other person's face. You may be used to just asking directly, but in Japan a question with no opener makes people feel interrupted, even a little as if they're being ordered around.
站员一天被问几百次路，最怕的是对方听不懂又不说。你复述一遍、说一句「お忙しいとこ: Station attendants are asked for directions hundreds of times a day, and what they dread most is someone who doesn't understand but doesn't say so. If you repeat back what you heard and say 「お忙しいところ」, they'll breathe a sigh of relief: this person understood, and is considerate of me too. Next time you ask, they'll be more willing to tell you a little more.
东京站的站员一个早上要回答上百个问题，有时还要一边看着检票口、一边帮老人搬行李。: Tokyo Station attendants answer more than a hundred questions in a single morning, sometimes while keeping an eye on the ticket gates and helping elderly passengers with their luggage. They say 「お気をつけて」 to everyone, and it isn't just a formality; it reflects a sincere spirit in Japanese service work: seeing passengers safely onto their trains is what the job is all about. What we can give back is to ask our questions clearly, listen carefully and repeat back what we heard, and say 「ありがとうございました」 sincerely when we leave. Many learners worry that their Japanese isn't good enough and would rather wander around the station for an hour than speak up. In fact, the people station staff welcome most are those who come and ask early: ask early, and you won't miss your train. Working up the courage to speak is the first step of any trip.
你想坐新干线，但还没买票，最自然的开口方式是？: You want to take the shinkansen but haven't bought a ticket yet. What's the most natural way to start?
先用「〜たいんですが」说明自己的情况，对方自然会告诉你怎么做。第二个太突兀，第三: Use 「〜たいんですが」 to explain your situation first, and the other person will naturally tell you what to do. The second option is too abrupt, and the third and fourth don't mean the right thing.
站员说「この通路をまっすぐ行って、右側です」，你最好怎么回应？: The station attendant says 「この通路をまっすぐ行って、右側です」. What's the best way to respond?
复述关键路线并用「ね」确认，对方能马上纠正你的误解，也知道你听懂了。: Repeating the key part of the route and confirming with 「ね」 lets the other person correct any misunderstanding right away, and also shows that you've understood.
「列車によって違います」是什么意思？: What does 「列車によって違います」 mean?
根据车次不同而不一样: It varies depending on the train
「〜によって違います」= 因……而不同。站员在告诉你要自己看显示屏确认具体站台。: 「〜によって違います」 means "it varies depending on (something)." The attendant is telling you to check the display board yourself for the exact track.
